**The Last Letter**

I found it in the bottom drawer of my grandmother’s desk, tucked between a yellowed recipe for peach cobbler and a faded photograph of my great-grandmother holding a baby. The envelope was thin, its edges brittle with age, the wax seal cracked. Inside was a single sheet of paper, written in a hand I didn’t recognize—neither mine nor hers.

*Dearest [Name],*

*I write this on the eve of my departure, though I know you will not read it until after I am gone. I have lived a long life, and in my final days, I have come to understand something I never did before: the weight of silence. You have always been the one who spoke for us, the one who carried the burdens of our family in your words. But I have realized that silence is not weakness—it is a choice, a quiet strength. You do not need to fill every moment with sound. You do not need to answer every question. You do not need to be the one who holds everything together.*

*I have loved you, [Name], in every way I could. I have loved you when you were angry, when you were kind, when you were lost. But I have also loved you when you were silent. And I hope, in the years to come, that you will find the same peace in that quiet.*

*With all my love,*
*[Grandmother’s Name]*

I sat there for a long time, the words sinking into me like a slow, heavy rain. My grandmother had always been the one who spoke for us, the one who told stories, the one who made sure everyone knew what was expected. And yet, in her final letter, she had chosen silence.

I thought about the times I had been silent too—when I didn’t want to say what I knew, when I didn’t want to be the one who carried the weight. I thought about the times I had spoken, only to realize later that I had said the wrong thing, that I had forced words where silence might have been better.

The letter was dated years ago, but it felt like it had been written yesterday. I folded it carefully, tucking it back into the drawer where it belonged. Maybe, just maybe, silence was the strength I had been searching for all along.
